competencies.justification: C-7.1 enumerates cultural elements, languages, art, philosophical ideas, values, clothing, cuisines, traditions and health practices, and the chapter's section list matches that enumeration almost item for item — 'Belief Systems' with bhakti and Sufism, 'Musical Traditions', 'From Walls to Paper — Miniature Paintings', 'Changing Landscapes — Gardens', 'Education and Knowledge Traditions', 'Growth of Literature and Language' with the development of Urdu, 'Developments in Science and Technology' naming Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani, 'Regional Architectural Developments', and 'Cultural Exchange in Daily Life' with its Food and Clothing subsections. More importantly, recognising commonality within that diversity is the chapter's fundamental organising argument, stated in the opening as three common patterns — continuation of traditional practices, patronage from rulers of various backgrounds, and active participation by people across all sections of society — and demonstrated everywhere: bhakti and Sufi traditions overlapping, Dara Shikoh championing the unity of the paths and having Upanishads translated into Persian, Amir Khusro developing the qawwali by fusing Indian, Persian and Arabic singing traditions, Rajput and Mughal painters exchanging style and technique, Mughal gardens borrowing the Persian charbagh while Amer Fort borrowed back, the samosa adapted from the Persian sambuseh and jalebi from zalabiyeh, the angrakha evolving from Persian court fashion, and Urdu forming from Hindavi with Arabic and Persian. Remove this competency and no chapter remains.

Rule 5(b) is satisfied and the chapter's own organising logic makes the continuity explicit, since Big Question 1 asks how Indian culture endured and continued to grow richer despite invasions and instability. 'Belief Systems' poses precisely this puzzle, asking why, unlike other parts of the world where a militant version of a ruler's faith suppressed indigenous faiths, the belief systems native to India continued alongside Islam more than a millennium later. 'The power of the bhakti tradition' answers it by showing a path crystallised by the 6th century reviving on pre-existing ground of Puranas, epics, temple visits and festivals. The Sufism section concludes that embedded traditions stayed alive while new ideas were integrated, sustained less by royal patronage than by popular participation, and records the Alvars and Nayanars' Divya Prabandham and Tiruvachakam still being recited. 'Musical Traditions — Continuation and Evolution' carries continuity in its heading and notes that Carnatic music continued to develop independently, largely unaffected by Persian and Arabic influence. 'Institutions of learning' records that decentralised jati and shreni systems remained largely unaffected by political turmoil and that Vijayanagara rulers were guided by purvamaryade, the following of previously established practices. 'Temple building and reconstruction' presents the rebuilding of Srirangam as the demonstration of that resilience.

Rule 5(b) is satisfied: identifying the reasons behind conflict and harmony among communities and their impact is the chapter's animating question, developed across multiple named sections. 'Belief Systems' states the conflict directly — a monotheistic Islam with one prophet set against a religion with several schools of thought and no single holy book, and invaders guided by their own version of Islam plundering and destroying some of the oldest and most sacred sites and temples — and then frames the whole chapter around why coexistence nonetheless followed. 'Regional saints and their messages' supplies part of the answer in Kabirdas decrying the rituals of both Hinduism and Islam and in Guru Nanak's message of one God preserved alongside the hymns of several Hindu saints in the Guru Granth Sahib, with a student activity on the Kabir doha that compares ground wheat with the dissolving of the difference between Ram and Rahim. 'Sufism' identifies the bridge, showing Sufis adopting yogic and Vedantic techniques and Bhakti and Sufi traditions overlapping. 'The case of Dara Shikoh' shows the counter-current, an advocate of Hindu-Muslim harmony persecuted, accused of heresy and executed by Aurangzeb. The closing recap names bhakti as a unifying force during political instability and Sufi saints as a valuable bridge between cultures.

Rule 5(a) is satisfied. 'Women in Society — Contextual Variations in Their Role and Status' is a dedicated, architecturally distinct named section that could stand alone as a learning unit on inequality, and it requires the student to explain regional and temporal variation rather than merely note it: it opens with Abu Zaidu-l Hasan's tenth-century observation that Indian princes allowed their women to be seen unveiled at court, then traces how invasions and military campaigns from the twelfth century saw women and children imprisoned and sold as slaves in West and Central Asian markets, some women committing jauhar, and how attempts to protect them reduced women's public appearance so that purdah and the ghunghat spread in parts of north India. It sets seclusion in royal Muslim households against Razia Sultan leading campaigns personally and appearing unveiled at court, acts that fuelled the conspiracy ending her reign, against Nur Jahan issuing royal orders and having coins minted in her name, and against south India where elite women issued grants, donated villages and built community halls and wells. Its activities require students to recall other women who went against the grain, to draw conclusions about women's economic and social status from Fernao Nunes's account, and to imagine a twenty-second-century historian writing about girls and women today. 'Regional saints and their messages' adds caste inequality, with Ravidas born into a family of leather-workers writing poetry that broke down rigid walls around varna and jati.

Rule 5(a) is satisfied: 'Developments in Science and Technology' is a dedicated named section whose entire subject is India's contributions to matters studied within the curriculum, explained in an integrated manner alongside those matters rather than asserted separately. It records the production of pure zinc by a distillation process employed for the first time in the world; Narayana Pandita's fourteenth-century Ganitakaumudi with its original developments; Madhava's series expansion for trigonometric functions and exact value of pi as an infinite series, both world firsts; the Kerala School of Astronomy and Mathematics producing important works into the nineteenth century; and Nilakantha Somayaji's planetary model of 1500 in which Mercury and Venus orbited the Sun, decades before Copernicus's heliocentric model of 1543. It adds applied chemistry in refrigeration, the rose-based Itr Jahangir and saltpetre used for gunpowder and for cooling water, and the transmission of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani through texts, oral tradition and palm-leaf manuscripts. 'Institutions of learning' records the Kerala School laying the seeds of infinite series and calculus, and 'The case of Dara Shikoh' records that his Persian translations of fifty-two Upanishads later reached Europe and influenced leading philosophers and thinkers in the nineteenth century.

Rule 6 is satisfied. 'Women in Society — Contextual Variations in Their Role and Status' contains a designated activity whose primary subject is primary-source interpretation and which requires an analytical operation on the source: students read Fernao Nunes's account of the vocations of women in the Vijayanagar king's staff and must draw conclusions about those women's economic and social status. The same section opens from a second primary source, the tenth-century Arab chronicler Abu Zaidu-l Hasan, and cites the wall engravings at Hampi and inscriptions recording temple donations by queens and wealthy women. 'Institutions of learning' uses the Italian traveller Pietro Della Valle's 1623 account of schools teaching reading, writing and arithmetic in coastal Karnataka, qualified by the observation that a school then was more likely a priest's house or a temple mandapa. 'From Walls to Paper — Miniature Paintings' cites Abul Fazl's praise of Hindu painters in the Ain-i-Akbari and requires students to compare the miniatures shown for similarities, differences, changes and retentions. These are source-interpretation tasks distributed through sections organised around cultural themes.

Rule 6 is satisfied. The chapter is organised thematically rather than as a change narrative, but several named sections contain designated passages whose primary subject is a major change and its impact on society. 'From Walls to Paper — Miniature Paintings' explains the shift from cave art and the Ajanta murals to mural and fresco forms and then, after paper reached India in the tenth or eleventh century, from walls to paper, and the consequent emergence of Mughal miniature painting as a distinct genre. 'The development of Urdu' traces a language forming in the Ganga-Yamuna plains from Hindi and Hindavi with Arabic and Persian words, replacing Persian as an official language under the British and diverging into Dakhini south of the Deccan. 'Institutions of learning' analyses the destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila during the late twelfth-century invasions as an immense cultural loss that dispersed learned scholars and disrupted an entire ecosystem, with a student activity requiring learners to consider its impact on education and knowledge in India and the world. 'Women in Society' traces the spread of purdah and the ghunghat as a change following the twelfth-century campaigns.
